triage.name: Bladder Cancer
triage.reason: Painless hematuria with smoking history; diagnosis reachable by history, urinalysis and cystoscopy workup.

demographics: About 3–4 times more common in men than women
More common in White individuals than in Black, Hispanic or Asian individuals in US data
Incidence rises steadily with age; it is uncommon before age 40
More common in developed countries and in regions with a history of industrial chemical exposure

risk_factors.text: Cigarette smoking (current or former); the single largest modifiable risk factor
Occupational exposure to aromatic amines (dyes, rubber, leather, printing, textiles, paint, truck driving)
Chronic bladder irritation: long-term indwelling catheter, recurrent urinary tract infections, chronic cystitis
Prior pelvic radiation or cyclophosphamide chemotherapy
Chronic Schistosoma haematobium infection (squamous cell histology)
Lynch syndrome or other inherited cancer predisposition

comorbidities: Chronic indwelling urinary catheter or neurogenic bladder
Prior pelvic malignancy treated with radiation
family_history: Bladder cancer in a first-degree relative
Lynch syndrome or other hereditary cancer syndrome
social_history: Pipe, cigar or smokeless tobacco use
Occupational history in dye, rubber, leather, textile, printing, paint or trucking industries

chief_complaints.text: I have to pee all the time and it burns
My urine looks like tea or cola
I've been having lower back pain

hpi.onset: Gradual and often unnoticed; blood is frequently first seen on a routine urinalysis or noticed as a change in urine color
hpi.duration: Weeks to months of intermittent symptoms before presentation
hpi.progression: Hematuria is typically intermittent and painless, so it may come and go; over time episodes become more frequent or heavier, and irritative voiding symptoms may develop or worsen
hpi.location: Blood originates in the bladder; discomfort, when present, is suprapubic or in the lower back/flank
hpi.radiation: Usually none; if a tumor obstructs a ureter, flank pain may radiate to the groin
hpi.quality: Gross hematuria described as pink, red, tea- or cola-colored urine; voiding symptoms described as burning, urgency and frequency
hpi.severity: Often mild and intermittent; can become heavy with clots causing urinary retention
hpi.timing: Hematuria is classically intermittent and painless; irritative symptoms may be constant or worse with voiding
aggravating: Voiding may worsen burning or urgency
relieving: Symptoms may resolve on their own between episodes, which can falsely reassure

associated_symptoms.text: Microscopic hematuria found on urinalysis without visible blood
Fatigue or pallor from chronic blood loss
Weight loss, bone pain or leg swelling suggesting advanced disease

pertinent_negatives: Severe colicky flank pain radiating to the groin
Recent trauma to the back or abdomen
Recent vigorous exercise before the blood appeared
New anticoagulant started just before the bleeding
Painless hematuria that resolves completely and never recurs

argues_against: High fever with flank pain suggesting pyelonephritis

positives.text: Getting up at night to urinate

argues_against: Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin suggesting a stone
Fever with dysuria suggesting urinary tract infection
Gastrointestinal bleeding as the source of blood
Mechanical back pain worsened by movement
A systemic bleeding disorder as the cause of hematuria

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with nonspecific fatigue, anemia or recurrent urinary tract infections rather than visible blood; irritative symptoms are more often attributed to benign prostatic hyperplasia or aging.
Hematuria may be attributed to chronic kidney disease or glomerular disease, delaying recognition of a bladder tumor; imaging and cystoscopy are still needed.
missing_classic_features: Isolated painless hematuria with normal renal function

atypical.how_it_differs: Irritative voiding symptoms and hematuria are more likely to be treated as infection first, and malignancy may be missed if symptoms improve with antibiotics.
Hematuria is often attributed to urinary tract infection or pregnancy-related changes; gross hematuria in pregnancy still requires urologic evaluation.

general.mild: Well-appearing, comfortable, no distress; may look well despite visible blood in the urine
general.moderate: Mildly fatigued or pale; comfortable at rest, no acute distress
general.severe: Ill-appearing, pale, fatigued; may have suprapubic discomfort or visible hematuria with clots
general.critical: Toxic or cachectic-appearing, pale and diaphoretic; may be in distress from clot retention, obstruction or metastatic disease

findings.maneuver: Inspect the urine in the collection container or ask about the color of the stream
findings.finding: Pink, red, tea- or cola-colored urine; blood may be visible throughout the stream
Mild suprapubic tenderness without guarding or rebound

findings.maneuver: Palpate and percuss the suprapubic area
findings.finding: A distended, palpable bladder suggesting clot retention or outlet obstruction
Unilateral costovertebral angle tenderness from ureteral obstruction by tumor

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen and suprapubic region deeply
findings.finding: A firm suprapubic or pelvic mass suggesting a large or locally advanced tumor

findings.maneuver: Palpate the inguinal lymph node basins
Inspect the conjunctivae and oral mucosa
findings.finding: Pallor suggesting anemia from chronic blood loss
Prostate may be enlarged or nodular from coexisting benign prostatic hyperplasia or prostate cancer; a firm bladder mass may be palpable anteriorly in advanced disease

findings.maneuver: Measure temperature and assess for systemic signs of infection
Ask about and assess for colicky flank pain radiating to the groin
findings.finding: Absence of severe colicky flank pain

labs.caveat: Hematuria is the key finding; it may be intermittent, so a single negative dipstick does not exclude bladder cancer.
Microscopy confirms true hematuria and helps exclude myoglobinuria or hemoglobinuria.
Anemia is usually from chronic blood loss; a normal hemoglobin does not exclude cancer.
Elevated when a tumor obstructs a ureter or in coexisting chronic kidney disease; needed before contrast imaging and chemotherapy.
Sterile pyuria can occur with bladder cancer and may be mistaken for urinary tract infection.
Pyuria without a positive culture should raise concern for tumor.
Elevated with bone metastases or biliary obstruction.

imaging.study: CT urography (CT abdomen and pelvis with and without IV contrast)
imaging.preferred_when: Adults with hematuria and risk factors for urothelial cancer; evaluates the upper tracts and bladder

findings.text: Focal bladder wall mass or thickening that enhances
Filling defect within the bladder lumen
Enlarged pelvic or retroperitoneal lymph nodes
Upper tract urothelial lesion or synchronous tumor
No bladder abnormality seen (small or flat tumors can be missed)

imaging.preferred_when: First-line in some patients, pregnancy, or when contrast cannot be given

findings.text: Bladder mass or focal wall thickening
Normal study (small or flat tumors are easily missed)

imaging.study: MRI abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Contraindication to CT contrast or staging of muscle-invasive disease

findings.text: Bladder mass with depth of invasion into the muscularis propria
Extravascular extension or adjacent organ involvement
Pulmonary nodules or masses suggesting metastasis

imaging.preferred_when: Staging of muscle-invasive or high-grade disease
Bone pain or elevated alkaline phosphatase in muscle-invasive disease

initial.why: Confirms hematuria and looks for infection or other causes
Assesses anemia from chronic blood loss and baseline counts
Baseline renal function before contrast imaging and treatment
Noninvasive first look at the urinary tract
initial.only_if: CT urography is not immediately available or contrast is contraindicated

confirmatory.test: Cystoscopy with biopsy or transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT)
confirmatory.why: Direct visualization and tissue diagnosis; the definitive test for bladder cancer

supporting.test: CT urography (CT abdomen and pelvis with and without IV contrast)
supporting.why: Evaluates the upper tracts and stages the bladder tumor
Helps detect high-grade urothelial carcinoma; a positive result supports the diagnosis but a negative result does not exclude it

supporting.only_if: muscle-invasive or high-grade disease is confirmed

supporting.test: MRI abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
supporting.why: Local staging when CT contrast cannot be given

supporting.only_if: bone pain or elevated alkaline phosphatase

not_indicated.why: Not routinely needed unless infection is suspected; a positive culture does not exclude cancer
Not a substitute for CT staging; low yield for small metastases
No role in hematuria or suspected bladder cancer
Not part of bladder cancer workup; prostate cancer is a separate evaluation

decision_points: Any adult with gross hematuria or persistent microscopic hematuria should be referred for cystoscopy and upper tract imaging
Do not attribute hematuria to urinary tract infection until infection is treated and hematuria is rechecked
Check renal function before contrast-enhanced CT
Cystoscopy with biopsy is required for tissue diagnosis even when imaging is abnormal

differential.name: Urinary tract infection
differential.why_considered: Hematuria with dysuria, frequency and urgency is the most common reason bladder cancer is initially missed

history: Acute onset over hours to a few days rather than weeks to months
Fever, chills or flank pain
Symptoms resolve completely with antibiotics
No history of smoking or occupational chemical exposure
labs: Positive urine culture with a single organism
imaging: No bladder mass on ultrasound or CT

differential.name: Kidney stones
differential.why_considered: Hematuria with flank or lower abdominal pain is a classic presentation of urolithiasis

history: Sudden, severe colicky flank pain radiating to the groin
Patient writhes and cannot get comfortable
Prior stone episodes
Nausea and vomiting with the pain
imaging: Radio-opaque stone in the ureter or kidney on non-contrast CT
Hydronephrosis on the affected side without a bladder mass

differential.name: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
differential.why_considered: Older men with frequency, urgency, nocturia and occasional hematuria often have BPH rather than cancer

history: Gradual onset of hesitancy, weak stream, dribbling and nocturia over years
No gross hematuria or only trace hematuria
No weight loss or bone pain
exam: Enlarged, smooth, non-nodular prostate on digital rectal exam
imaging: Enlarged prostate with post-void residual urine
No bladder mass on ultrasound or CT

differential.name: Prostate cancer
differential.why_considered: Older men with hematuria, urinary symptoms and an abnormal prostate exam may have prostate cancer rather than bladder cancer
differential.trigger: Hard or nodular prostate on digital rectal exam, or elevated PSA

history: Urinary symptoms with bone pain, especially back or hip pain
Family history of prostate cancer
No gross hematuria early in the course
exam: Hard, nodular or asymmetrical prostate on digital rectal exam
labs: Elevated alkaline phosphatase with bone metastases
imaging: Sclerotic bone lesions on bone scan
Bladder involvement by direct extension rather than a primary bladder mass

differential.name: Kidney cancer
differential.why_considered: Renal cell carcinoma can present with hematuria and flank pain, and is a common upper tract malignancy in older adults
differential.trigger: Flank mass, hematuria and a renal mass on imaging

history: Flank pain and a palpable abdominal mass
Weight loss, fever or night sweats
Paraneoplastic symptoms such as hypercalcemia or polycythemia
exam: Varicocele, especially on the right side
imaging: Enhancing renal cortical mass on CT or MRI

differential.name: Overactive bladder
differential.why_considered: Frequency, urgency and nocturia overlap with the irritative symptoms of bladder cancer

history: Chronic urgency and frequency without hematuria
No smoking or occupational exposure history
Symptoms fluctuate with fluid intake, caffeine and stress
imaging: Normal bladder on ultrasound or CT

differential.name: Interstitial cystitis
differential.why_considered: Chronic suprapubic pain, urgency and frequency can mimic bladder cancer, especially in women

history: Chronic pelvic pain relieved by voiding
Symptoms for months to years without gross hematuria
No smoking history
labs: Sterile urine with no hematuria or only trace blood
imaging: Normal bladder mucosa on cystoscopy except for glomerulations or Hunner lesions
No mass on CT or ultrasound

differential.name: Glomerulonephritis
differential.why_considered: Hematuria with red blood cell casts and proteinuria can be mistaken for a urologic source of bleeding
differential.trigger: Red blood cell casts, proteinuria or rising creatinine with hematuria

history: Recent upper respiratory or skin infection
Dark, cola-colored urine with edema
No smoking history
labs: Red blood cell casts on urine microscopy
Low complement levels in post-infectious glomerulonephritis
imaging: Normal bladder and upper tracts on ultrasound or CT

severity.mild: Non-muscle-invasive disease (Ta, T1, carcinoma in situ): painless hematuria or microscopic hematuria only, normal renal function, no anemia, no obstruction, well-appearing
severity.moderate: Larger or recurrent non-muscle-invasive tumor or early muscle-invasive disease: visible hematuria with clots, mild anemia, irritative voiding symptoms, no distant metastasis
severity.severe: Muscle-invasive or locally advanced disease: heavy hematuria with clot retention, hydronephrosis from ureteral obstruction, anemia, weight loss, pelvic pain
severity.critical: Metastatic or obstructing disease with life-threatening complications: clot retention with bladder tamponade, acute kidney injury from bilateral obstruction, sepsis from urinary infection, spinal cord compression or hypercalcemia from bone metastases

red_flags.finding: Gross hematuria with clots causing inability to urinate
red_flags.meaning: Clot retention or bladder tamponade; needs urgent bladder irrigation and urology evaluation

red_flags.finding: Flank pain with rising creatinine and hydronephrosis
red_flags.meaning: Ureteral obstruction by tumor; may require urgent decompression

red_flags.finding: Fever, chills and hypotension with hematuria
red_flags.meaning: Urosepsis; needs cultures, antibiotics and urgent urology involvement

red_flags.finding: New severe back pain with leg weakness or incontinence
red_flags.meaning: Spinal cord compression from bone metastasis; a neurologic emergency

red_flags.finding: Confusion, polyuria or constipation with elevated calcium
red_flags.meaning: Hypercalcemia of malignancy; requires urgent correction

red_flags.finding: Weight loss, bone pain or night sweats
red_flags.meaning: Suggests metastatic disease and warrants staging imaging

complications.name: Acute urinary retention from clot retention
clues: Inability to void with suprapubic pain

complications.name: Progression to muscle-invasive disease
clues: Increasing tumor stage on repeat resection

special_populations.differences: More likely to present with nonspecific fatigue, anemia or recurrent urinary tract infections rather than visible blood; more comorbidity limits treatment options and increases perioperative risk.

Hematuria may be attributed to chronic kidney disease; renal function must be checked before contrast imaging and chemotherapy, and nephroureterectomy may be contraindicated if the other kidney is impaired.
Irritative symptoms and hematuria are more often treated as infection first, delaying diagnosis; cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide exposure increases risk.
Gross hematuria in pregnancy still requires urologic evaluation; ultrasound is preferred over CT to avoid fetal radiation, and cystoscopy can be performed safely when needed.
Higher risk of urinary tract infection and poorer wound healing after surgery; glucose control should be optimized before radical cystectomy.
Higher surgical risk and technically more difficult radical cystectomy; smoking-related comorbidities are common.

cancer.screening: There is no recommended screening test for bladder cancer in the general population. The USPSTF recommends against screening for bladder cancer in asymptomatic adults. Evaluation is triggered by symptoms, especially gross hematuria or persistent microscopic hematuria, or by high-risk occupational exposure.
cancer.pathology: More than 90% of bladder cancers in the United States are urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma. Other types include squamous cell carcinoma (associated with chronic irritation or Schistosoma haematobium), adenocarcinoma, and rare small cell or sarcomatoid variants. Tumors are classified as non-muscle-invasive (Ta, T1, carcinoma in situ) or muscle-invasive (T2 or higher). Grade is reported as low or high grade, with high grade carrying a much higher risk of progression.
cancer.staging_concepts: Staging uses the TNM system. Ta is non-invasive papillary, T1 invades the lamina propria, T2 invades the muscularis propria, T3 invades perivesical fat, and T4 invades adjacent organs such as the prostate, uterus, vagina, pelvic wall or abdominal wall. Nodal stage reflects pelvic lymph node involvement and M stage reflects distant metastasis. Muscle invasion is the key dividing line because it determines whether treatment is bladder-preserving or radical cystectomy. Cystoscopy with transurethral resection provides the tissue diagnosis and depth of invasion; CT or MRI of the abdomen and pelvis and CT of the chest complete staging.

key_questions.question: Have you noticed blood in your urine, and if so, what did it look like?
key_questions.looking_for: Painless gross hematuria described as pink, red, tea- or cola-colored; the cardinal presenting symptom

key_questions.question: Is the blood there all the time or does it come and go?
key_questions.looking_for: Intermittent bleeding that resolves between episodes, which can falsely reassure the patient

key_questions.question: Does it hurt when you urinate, or is the blood painless?
key_questions.looking_for: Painless hematuria strongly suggests malignancy; dysuria alone points toward infection or stones

key_questions.question: How long has this been going on?
key_questions.looking_for: Weeks to months of intermittent symptoms rather than an acute onset over hours to days

key_questions.question: Do you have to urinate more often, urgently, or get up at night to urinate?
key_questions.looking_for: Irritative voiding symptoms that may accompany or precede the hematuria

key_questions.question: Have you passed any clots, or had trouble urinating?
key_questions.looking_for: Clots causing inability to void suggests clot retention or bladder tamponade and needs urgent urology evaluation

key_questions.question: Have you had any fever, chills or flank pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever and chills suggest infection or urosepsis; severe colicky flank pain suggests a stone

key_questions.question: Have you ever smoked cigarettes, or do you still smoke?
key_questions.looking_for: Current or former smoking, the single largest modifiable risk factor

key_questions.question: What kind of work have you done? Any exposure to dyes, rubber, leather, printing, paint or trucking chemicals?
key_questions.looking_for: Occupational exposure to aromatic amines and related industrial chemicals

key_questions.question: Have you had urinary tract infections, kidney stones, or a long-term urinary catheter?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic bladder irritation, recurrent infections or indwelling catheter increasing risk

key_questions.question: Have you ever had radiation to the pelvis or chemotherapy such as cyclophosphamide?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior pelvic radiation or cyclophosphamide/ifosfamide exposure as risk factors

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had bladder cancer or another cancer syndrome?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of bladder cancer or an inherited cancer predisposition such as Lynch syndrome

key_questions.question: Have you had any weight loss, bone pain or night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Constitutional symptoms suggesting advanced or metastatic disease

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Excludes menstrual bleeding as the source and guides imaging choice in women of reproductive age

accepted_names: Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder
reasoning_points: Painless gross or microscopic hematuria in an older adult, especially a smoker or someone with occupational chemical exposure
Hematuria is typically intermittent, so a single negative urinalysis does not exclude the diagnosis
Irritative voiding symptoms such as frequency, urgency and dysuria may accompany the hematuria and can be mistaken for urinary tract infection
Urinalysis confirms blood without infection; sterile pyuria can occur and should raise concern for tumor
Risk factors include cigarette smoking, aromatic amine exposure, age over 60, male sex, chronic bladder irritation, prior pelvic radiation or cyclophosphamide, and family history
Cystoscopy with biopsy or transurethral resection is the definitive test for tissue diagnosis
CT urography evaluates the upper tracts and stages the tumor; ultrasound is an alternative when contrast cannot be given
Urine cytology supports but does not exclude the diagnosis; a negative result does not rule out cancer
Muscle invasion on pathology is the key dividing line that determines bladder-preserving therapy versus radical cystectomy

Look-alikes such as urinary tract infection, kidney stones, benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostate cancer, kidney cancer, overactive bladder, interstitial cystitis and glomerulonephritis must be considered and excluded

easy: Older man with a long smoking history
Painless gross hematuria described as tea- or cola-colored urine
Hematuria found on urinalysis with no signs of infection
Bladder mass seen on ultrasound or CT urography
Cystoscopy confirms a papillary bladder tumor
medium: Microscopic hematuria found incidentally on routine urinalysis without visible blood
Irritative voiding symptoms treated as urinary tract infection that do not fully resolve
Sterile pyuria on urinalysis with a negative urine culture
Older adult presenting with fatigue and anemia rather than visible blood
Occupational aromatic amine exposure without a smoking history
hard: Hematuria attributed to benign prostatic hyperplasia or chronic kidney disease, delaying recognition of a tumor
Small or flat carcinoma in situ missed on ultrasound and CT, requiring cystoscopy for diagnosis
Patient with a coexisting urinary tract infection whose hematuria persists after antibiotics
Gross hematuria in pregnancy attributed to pregnancy-related changes or infection
Presentation with clot retention, hydronephrosis or metastatic bone pain rather than isolated hematuria
Immunocompromised patient whose irritative symptoms improve with antibiotics but whose hematuria recurs
